title: Vectorizing Philosophers
subtitle: How the language a thinker spoke shifted under them
question: When a philosopher says substance, how much of what they mean is theirs, and how much is just the century talking?
scope: Every philosopher inherits a vocabulary and hands on a different one. The words survive — substance, reason, freedom, subject — while what they point at moves underneath, which is why reading an old argument in a modern sense is the most reliable way to misread it.

This topic measures that drift instead of asserting it. Texts are embedded in vector space, so a term can be located rather than glossed: near what, in whose work, in which century. A concept becomes a trajectory you can plot.
Three lenses, because the drift has three shapes. A concept moving across everyone. A thinker moving across a life. A century moving across its own vocabulary.

method.name: Corpus assembly
method.note: Public-domain editions, aligned by work and date of composition rather than date of printing.

method.name: Diachronic embeddings
method.note: Time-sliced vector spaces, aligned so that a term's position is comparable across centuries.

method.name: Semantic drift
method.note: Measuring how far a concept travels, and which neighbours it swaps along the way.

method.name: Translation control
method.note: Comparing translations of the same source, so drift in the translator is not read as drift in the thinker.
